Galitsky, C., Martin, N., Worrell, E. and Lehman, B. (2003). Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for Breweries: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers. Report LBNL-50934, Ernest Orlando Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA, September 2003. No DOI or URL printed.

Locators are printed page numbers (PDF page = printed + 8; front matter in roman numerals). An ENERGY STAR measure catalogue; almost every number is reprinted from other sources (Hackensellner 2000, Weinzierl et al. 2000, Seldeslachts 1999, NOVEM, CADDET, EIA 1997...), named at the end of each note. The guide reports energy per U.S. beer barrel (31 gallons, footnote 2) and states kBtu are HHV (footnote 4); per-barrel values are converted to GJ/m3 or kWh/m3 of beer with an explicit formula (x*1.055056/117.347765; x/0.117347765); printed per-hl values are multiplied by 10. Main file (25 technologies, 28 examples): brewhouse step intensities (decoction and infusion mashing fuel; conventional wort kettle fuel 44-46 kBtu/bbl (Germany) and 36 kBtu/bbl (Merlin comparison) and conventional mashing+boiling 92 kBtu/bbl (Interbrew trials)); efficient wort boiling (thermal VR motive steam per barrel of WATER EVAPORATED; mechanical VR fuel and electricity; Merlin with and without energy storage; low-pressure boiling steam (mashing+boiling scope, per barrel cast wort); wort stripping, two contexts); single- and two-stage wort coolers (electricity); fermentation CO2 (biogenic, 3-4 kg/hl); microfiltration electricity (generic, PG&E); RO and dialysis dealcoholization utilities cost; tunnel and flash pasteurizers (thermal energy, flash capex, O&M); keg-washer purge steam (kg/keg); boiler efficiency 85% and average U.S. brewery fuel 212 kBtu/bbl (authors' assumptions, Table 8 note B); absorption chiller steam (kg/kW, time basis unstated); ultra-high-pressure sterilization cost; anaerobic wastewater digester (biogas output in _flows). _measures.csv: every row of Tables 8-9 (PRIMARY kBtu/barrel savings, electricity x3.08, and payback) plus quantified case studies from Sects. 6-8 as printed. _other-values.csv: Tables 2-4 sector statistics, the 122 kBtu/bbl electricity assumption (apparently primary), tunnel pasteurization per 1000 bottles, primary-energy and percentage items, CHP plant sizes, maintenance costs. Not loaded: Figures 1-6 (charts only), Appendix I-IV (brewery list, management checklists), qualitative measures and future technologies without numbers (immobilized yeast, continuous wort boiling, hydrocyclones), water and material measures except where they carry a cost/payback. All costs: price year not stated, publication year 2003 used; underlying sources date 1993-2001. Heating value: HHV per footnote 4 for kBtu values; the Brand mash-filter saving is explicitly LHV.

(1) Barrel conversions inconsistent: footnote 2 gives 1 barrel = 1.2 hl, footnote 4 says divide by 0.85 barrel/hl (1.176 hl), the exact 31-gallon barrel is 1.1735 hl (used). (2) MVR electricity printed 0.3-2.8 kWh/barrel (0.1-0.7 kWh/hl) - the hl figures do not match; 'per barrel evaporate' leaves the denominator ambiguous. (3) Merlin electricity '0.02 kWh/barrel' and low-pressure 0.02 vs 0.01 kWh/hl are implausibly small for wort boiling. (4) Table 8 note B: electricity 122 kBtu/barrel (30.5 kWh/hl) is evidently primary, mislabelled as consumption. (5) Grolsch anaerobic saving printed '11.9 kBtu/barrel (10.2 kBtu/hl)' - second unit should be MJ/hl. (6) Food sector energy '1585 TBtu (1.7 MJ)' unit slip (p.9). (7) Burnett and Rolfe keg washer: heat-exchanger saving 0.88-1.46 kg steam/keg exceeds the 0.4-0.8 kg/keg purge steam it is added to. (8) Table 8/9 savings are primary energy, not final. (9) Spelling 'Steineker' for Steinecker; table list skips Table 7.
